source.title: The interplay between domain specialization and model size: a case study in the legal domain
source.authors: Roseval Malaquias; Ramon Pires; T. Almeida; K. Sakiyama; R. Romero; Rodrigo Nogueira

record.file_problem: none noted; the supplied text contains the paper through its references.
record.tranche_reason: Tests scaling-related behavior in continued pretraining on filtered domain-specific versus unfiltered text, using Qwen2.5 models and downstream exam perplexity rather than the original held-out pretraining-loss measurement.
record.gate_note: The study evaluates correct-answer-token perplexity on MCQA exams and fits or describes trends against model size and compute. It does not report held-out pretraining cross-entropy results. Scaling-law claims cited from other work are not recorded as findings. Results below use the study's reported comparisons and trends; individual plotted PPL values are not transcribed in the text.
record.test_reason: The study continues pretraining of Qwen2.5 1.5B–14B models and fits power laws of downstream MCQA correct-letter perplexity against parameter count. It does this for five test suites and three regimes (specialized, general, base), so it bears on V6 in a new setting. It reports no held-out pretraining loss. Its 'optimal model size vs compute' fit (Fig. 3) does not find the loss-minimising N at fixed compute. It regresses model size on the compute each fixed-size model used to reach its minimum domain perplexity, so it does not test V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that, under fixed compute, domain-specialized continued pretraining beats general continued pretraining on target-domain exams at all sizes from 1.5B to 14B. They report that the gap persists along a power law: it is not growing for legal, though it appears to grow for medical and accounting. Specialization becomes more sample-efficient with size (SGER 1.6× to 4.3×), larger specialized models forget less, and the model size needed under a fixed budget rises more steeply with specialization. They note four points per fit, one dataset, and that they do not formalize a scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: Continued pretraining of pretrained Qwen2.5 models on Portuguese web data, with specialized filtered subsets versus the unfiltered corpus; evaluates downstream MCQA answer-token perplexity and fits trends over 1.5B–14B sizes. The original scaling-law studies measure held-out language-modeling loss in controlled scaling sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Training regime (specialized versus general) changes the reported model-size/compute fit; target domain and test suite change which regime performs better. The authors identify data volume and classifier limitations as relevant constraints.

fits_no_version.finding: Specialized-vs-general efficiency ratio (compute to reach minimum domain perplexity) rises from 1.6× at 1.5B to 4.3× at 14B. Tokens to minimum fall from 33.6B to 12.6B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In compute-constrained continued pretraining, domain-filtered data reaches minimum domain perplexity with relatively less compute as model size grows.

fits_no_version.finding: Model size regressed on compute-to-minimum-perplexity gives N ∝ C^1.64 (legal-specialized) versus C^1.06 (general).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The data regime (domain filtering) changes the relation between model size and the compute needed to reach minimum downstream perplexity in continued pretraining.

record.problems: The study uses one dataset, ClueWeb 2022, and acknowledges possible noise from its content classifiers. The authors state that each fitted power law has only four data points, the scale range is limited to 1.5B–14B, and smaller models were not useful on the exams. No uncertainty estimates or statistical tests are reported for the plotted trends. The evaluations are downstream MCQA exams rather than held-out pretraining loss.
record.rows_left_out: No additional separately reported quantitative scaling outcomes were omitted. Figures 1–5 do not provide individual numeric PPL values in the text, so the rows record only the stated trends and the explicitly printed Figure 3 fit equations.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss; only the probability of the MCQA answer letter.
No extrapolation from small runs to much larger ones; the range is 1.5B–14B, about one order of magnitude.
No fixed-compute sweep over N and D; the Fig. 3 fit is not a compute-optimal allocation.
No variation of shape at fixed parameter count.
Text only; continued pretraining is measured with downstream perplexity, not loss.
Prediction from pretraining loss and extrapolation beyond 14B are not tested. Sizes are separately pretrained Qwen2.5 base models, so model scale is confounded with each base model's own pretraining.
No comparison of parameter counting, schedules or fitting methods for loss laws or compute-optimal splits.

missing.what: Fitted exponents of MCQA perplexity versus N, per regime, for each test suite: legal 0.2062/0.2155/0.1525; medical 0.2216/0.2086/0.2029; accounting 0.1744/0.1639/0.1220; MMLU 0.2668/0.2242/0.1765; new general 0.2136/0.1939/0.2111. Order follows the legend (specialized, general, base). Coefficients are garbled in the extracted text.
Statement that models under 1.5B score no better than chance on the exams, so they were excluded from the fits.

record.verdict_notes: Only V6 is tested, and only weakly. The evidence is four sizes spanning under one order of magnitude, with no uncertainty reported. The size axis is confounded with separately pretrained base models; the base-model fits show the same power-law form, so the trend is largely inherited from Qwen2.5's own scaling. The record's V3 and V7 links were removed because Fig. 3 is not a compute-optimal allocation analysis. Its name 'optimal model size' is the authors' label for compute-to-minimum per fixed size.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep; the reported perplexity is for the token representing the correct MCQA answer.
No small-run fit is tested against runs orders of magnitude larger.

The study fits model size against compute in a legal-domain continued-pretraining setting, but does not establish a token-count-versus-compute power law. Its loss criterion is downstream exam perplexity, not held-out pretraining loss.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The study uses continued pretraining on text, but does not test whether the same held-out pretraining-loss power law transfers to other modalities or regimes.
The study evaluates downstream MCQA performance across model sizes, but does not test prediction from pretraining loss or extrapolation to substantially larger models.

The study compares legal-specialized and general training curves, but does not vary parameter-counting conventions, fit methods, or training schedules, and does not test curve bending away from a power law.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 legal-specialized model
rows.operation_detail: Measured the specialized-to-general efficiency ratio at the checkpoint with minimum legal-test perplexity.
rows.measure: Specialized-to-General Efficiency Ratio (SGER), comparing compute used to reach minimum perplexity.
rows.baseline: General model's compute to reach minimum perplexity; ratio reference is 1×.
rows.value: SGER increases from 1.6× at 1.5B parameters to 4.3× at 14B parameters; the 1.5B specialized model requires 33.6B tokens to reach its minimum perplexity.
rows.note: The stated SGER and token count concern downstream legal-test perplexity and sample efficiency, not the claimed pretraining-loss allocation law.
rows.check: SGER is a ratio of compute to reach minimum perplexity between two data regimes. It is not a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation, so it should not be linked to V3.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 legal-specialized model
rows.operation_detail: Measured the specialized-to-general efficiency ratio at the checkpoint with minimum legal-test perplexity.
rows.measure: Specialized-to-General Efficiency Ratio (SGER), comparing compute used to reach minimum perplexity.
rows.baseline: General model's compute to reach minimum perplexity; ratio reference is 1×.
rows.value: SGER increases from 1.6× at 1.5B parameters to 4.3× at 14B parameters; the 14B specialized model requires 12.6B tokens to reach its minimum perplexity and achieves lower perplexity using 4.3× less compute than its general counterpart.
rows.note: The SGER and token count refer to the legal exam's minimum-perplexity checkpoints.
rows.check: Same as r4: SGER at 14B (4.3×) is a sample-efficiency comparison between regimes, not V3's allocation law.

rows.subject: Qwen2.5 continued-pretraining models
rows.size_stated: 1.5B, 3B, 7B, and 14B parameters; fitted relation across four sizes
rows.operation_detail: Fit optimal model size against training compute for the legal-specialized regime.
rows.measure: Model size at the reported minimum legal-test perplexity as a function of training compute.
rows.value: Figure 3 labels the fit as N = 4.1918 × 10^25 × C^1.6420.
rows.note: The paper describes optimal model size as increasing more steeply with compute under specialization. Four data points are used.
rows.check: Fig. 3 fits N against compute-to-minimum-perplexity across four fixed Qwen2.5 sizes. N was not varied at fixed C, so this is not V3's loss-minimising N(C). The exponent of 1.64 (>1) is not comparable to Kaplan's or Hoffmann's exponents. The measure is downstream perplexity, so it does not bear on V7 either.

Lowest perplexity on the corresponding domain-specific test suite

rows.measure: Average perplexity of the correct answer letter on the original general-knowledge test suite.
rows.baseline: General-trained models at corresponding sizes; base models also shown.
rows.value: The text reports that, as model size increases, specialized models achieve lower perplexity than general models on this test suite.
rows.note: This is a downstream general-knowledge result; the authors attribute it to greater sample efficiency and fewer continued-pretraining steps.
rows.check: Value records the regime comparison only. Fig. 4 shows MMLU correct-letter perplexity falling as a power law in N, with exponents 0.2668, 0.2242 and 0.1765. Checkpoints were selected on the domain suite.

relationships.condition: Qwen2.5 1.5B–14B after continued pretraining (specialized, general and base); MCQA correct-letter perplexity on legal, medical, accounting, new-general Portuguese and MMLU suites.
relationships.reason: Each suite and regime is fit by a decreasing power law in N, with exponents about 0.12–0.27 (r1, r2, r3, r10, r11). The exponents are read from the figure fits, not from the row values; see missing.
relationships.display_finding: Correct-letter perplexity followed decreasing power laws in model size across every suite and regime, with fitted exponents around 0.12–0.27.
